clue.text: Gladiator acts badly, pinching you after fight

indicators.note: placement word: what follows comes later in the line of letters

parts.note: to spar is to box or fight

indicators.note: to pinch is to grip tightly between fingers, so one piece closes around another
something done badly is botched and disordered, so the letters come out jumbled

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged
U is text-speak for you

explanation.surface: A film gladiator hams it up, pinching a co-star after the fight scene.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gladiator' is the definition at the front; 'after' places the boxing word first, with the rearranged letters following it.
explanation.definitionFit: Spartacus was the Thracian slave who fought in Roman arenas and led a famous revolt.

clue.text: Steal underwear

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to move quietly or sneak, as in steal away
second meaning: a light undergarment worn beneath a dress

explanation.walkthrough: It reads like a knicker thief's charge sheet, but 'steal' means to move stealthily, not to rob.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both to creep away unnoticed and a woman's lightweight petticoat garment.

clue.text: Clobber vacuous reprobate in disgust

indicators.note: one thing set inside another, so these letters go within the larger word

parts.note: to appal is to fill with disgust or horror

indicators.note: vacuous means empty, so the word loses its contents and keeps only its two ends

parts.note: just the first and last letters of the word

explanation.surface: Someone wants to beat up an empty-headed scoundrel out of sheer revulsion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Clobber' looks like a verb meaning hit, but it is British slang for clothes.
explanation.definitionFit: Clobber is informal British slang for clothing or gear, and apparel is a formal word for garments.

clue.text: Cobblers climbing hill

indicators.note: in a down entry, climbing means reading from bottom to top, so the word runs backwards

parts.note: cobblers is British slang for nonsense, which is rot

explanation.surface: Shoemakers trudging up a hillside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cobblers' pretends to be shoemakers; it is British slang for rubbish talk, i.e. ROT, which reads upwards as TOR.
explanation.definitionFit: A tor is a rocky outcrop or craggy peak, especially on Dartmoor in south-west England.

clue.text: Employee of mine clipped dog

indicators.note: something clipped has had its tail end trimmed off, so the final letter goes

parts.note: a coal miner

explanation.surface: A worker at my colliery gave his dog a trim.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Clipped' suggests grooming the dog, but it trims the last letter from COLLIER.
explanation.definitionFit: The collie is a Scottish sheepdog breed, a herding animal familiar from Lassie.

clue.text: Reportedly watch coppers complete shift

indicators.note: what is reported is heard rather than read, so go by the sound of the word

parts.note: to watch is to see, and the ocean word sounds the same
coppers are low-value coins, small change

explanation.surface: A news report says the police are working a full shift on watch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Coppers' suggests police, but means copper coins, i.e. loose change.
explanation.definitionFit: A sea change, from Shakespeare's Tempest, is a profound transformation or total turnaround in something.

clue.text: Very much failing at romance at first

indicators.note: at first means at the very beginning, so only each word's opening letter counts

parts.note: the opening letter of each of the three words

explanation.surface: Someone confesses they were hopeless at love early on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Very much' works as an intensifier, as in 'far better'.
explanation.definitionFit: Used before a comparative, the adverb means by a large margin or to a great degree.

clue.text: Shaving stick on middle of shelf

indicators.note: in a down entry, one thing on another sits above it, so it comes first

parts.note: taking stick means taking criticism, which is flak

indicators.note: the middle is the centre point, so only the central letter of the word is kept

parts.note: the third of five letters

explanation.surface: A shaving stick is placed in the middle of the bathroom shelf.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shaving stick' looks like one item, but splits: 'Shaving' is the definition and 'stick' means criticism.
explanation.definitionFit: A flake is a thin sliver or chip shaved off something, like a wood shaving or paint chip.

clue.text: Careless misers ruined

indicators.note: something ruined is wrecked out of its proper shape, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Penny-pinchers who were sloppy with money ended up broke.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ruined' looks like the misers' fate, but it tells you to rearrange the word before it.
explanation.definitionFit: Remiss describes someone negligent in their duty, lax or inattentive, which is near-synonymous.

clue.text: Ignoring answer, sovereign is put in jeopardy

indicators.note: ignoring something means leaving it out, so a letter is dropped

parts.note: sovereign as an adjective means royal or imperial
A is the standard abbreviation for answer

explanation.surface: A monarch who won't respond to questions finds the throne at risk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sovereign' reads as a noun for a king, but the adjective sense, imperial, is wanted; dropping its A leaves IMPERIL.
explanation.definitionFit: To imperil is to endanger something, exposing it to risk or harm.

clue.text: Scare section of Territorial Army

indicators.note: a section is a portion cut from a larger whole, so the letters lie within the phrase

parts.note: found across the join of the two words

explanation.surface: A unit of Britain's volunteer reserve force gets a fright.
explanation.walkthrough: The Territorial Army is the UK's part-time military reserve; the letters run across the end of one word and the start of the next.
explanation.definitionFit: Alarm is a sudden fright or fearful apprehension, so it is a straight synonym for scare.

clue.text: Puritanism and fervour finally stopping gluttony

indicators.note: to stop a gap is to plug it, so one piece fills a hole inside another

parts.note: eating like a pig is gluttony

indicators.note: finally means at the end, so only the word's last letter is kept

parts.note: the final letter

explanation.surface: Religious zeal and passion eventually put an end to overeating.
explanation.walkthrough: R plugs PIGGISHNESS after its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Priggishness is smug moral self-righteousness, close to the strict, censorious attitude called puritanism.

clue.text: My gerbil sadly eating old crumbs

indicators.note: what eats something takes it inside, so one piece swallows another
things that go sadly go wrong, so the letters fall into disorder

parts.note: taken as written
O is a common abbreviation for old

explanation.surface: A pet gerbil is unhappily nibbling stale crumbs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crumbs' looks like the gerbil's food, but it is an exclamation of surprise; gorblimey is a Cockney oath from 'God blind me'.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are dated British exclamations of surprise or dismay, mild substitutes for swearing.

clue.text: Slight sign of intoxication

definitions.meaning: first meaning: an insult or disparaging remark
second meaning: blurred, indistinct speech from drinking

explanation.walkthrough: 'Slight' looks like an adjective meaning small, as in a slight sign, but it is a noun meaning an insult.
explanation.definitionFit: A slur is both a derogatory remark and the mumbled, run-together speech of a drunk person.

clue.text: Bouquet of autumn's last roses unwrapped

indicators.note: the last of something is its final element, so only the closing letter stays

parts.note: the final letter of the season

indicators.note: taking off the wrapping removes the outer layer, so both end letters go

parts.note: the flower word minus its first and last letters

explanation.surface: A bunch of the season's final roses, freshly taken out of their paper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bouquet' suggests flowers, but it is a wine-taster's word for aroma.
explanation.definitionFit: In wine tasting the nose is the smell or aroma of a wine, also called its bouquet.

clue.text: Fruit is a necessity when laid up

indicators.note: in a down entry, putting something up turns it to read bottom to top, so it runs backwards

parts.note: taken as written
a must is something essential
as can mean when, as in 'as I left'

explanation.surface: Fruit becomes essential when you are ill in bed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Laid up' suggests being sick in bed, but in a down clue it turns the letters upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A satsuma is a small, easy-peel citrus fruit of the mandarin type, originally from Japan.

clue.text: Cloudy over Pennsylvania and half of Quebec

parts.note: O is the cricket scorer's abbreviation for an over
PA is the postal abbreviation for the US state

indicators.note: half a word is one of its two equal parts, so only three of six letters stay

parts.note: the opening three letters of the province name

explanation.surface: A weather report: overcast skies above Pennsylvania and part of Quebec.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Over' reads as 'above' in the weather picture, but it gives O, the cricket abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: Opaque means not transparent, letting no light through, like murky or clouded glass or liquid.

clue.text: Almost worth supporting trade union in Pacific nation

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the final letter is left off
in a down entry, a support sits underneath, so this piece comes second

parts.note: TU is the standard abbreviation for trade union
worth and value are synonyms

explanation.surface: Something of near value backs a labour union in a Pacific country.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue, 'supporting' means sitting underneath, so the shortened word goes second.
explanation.definitionFit: Tuvalu is a small Polynesian island country in the South Pacific, formerly the Ellice Islands.

clue.text: Excitedly alter a toupee for royal household member

indicators.note: doing something excitedly means agitated and jumbled, so the letters are shaken up

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An eager stylist adjusts a hairpiece for someone working at the palace.
explanation.walkthrough: The Poet Laureate is formally appointed by the British monarch as part of the Royal Household.
explanation.definitionFit: The post is an honorary appointment within the sovereign's household, writing verse for state occasions.

clue.text: Dash ultimately exhausted antelope

parts.note: dash in the sense of flair and verve is elan

indicators.note: ultimately means in the end, so only the word's final letter is used

parts.note: the final letter

explanation.surface: An antelope makes a final dash and collapses, worn out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dash' looks like a sprint, but it means stylish verve.
explanation.definitionFit: The eland is a large African antelope with spiralled horns, the biggest of its family.

clue.text: Current covers of expurgated diary

indicators.note: a book's covers are at its front and back, so only the first and last letters stay

parts.note: first and last letters
first and last letters

explanation.surface: The front and back covers of a censored, up-to-date journal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Current' looks like an adjective describing the diary, but it is a noun for moving water.
explanation.definitionFit: An eddy is a swirling circular flow of water or air, a small current running against the main stream.

clue.text: Misgiving of peer dropping ecstasy with male

indicators.note: with means alongside, so the next piece is simply added on
to drop something is to let it go, so that letter is removed

parts.note: a peer is one's equal
E is slang for the drug ecstasy
M is the abbreviation for male

explanation.surface: A man's doubts about a nobleman who has given up drugs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Peer' suggests a lord, but it means an equal.
explanation.definitionFit: A qualm is an uneasy feeling of doubt or conscience, the same thing as a misgiving.

clue.text: Hound leaving lead on a stone floor

indicators.note: to leave the lead is to lose the front position, so the opening letter goes
one piece placed on another is attached to it, so they join end to end

parts.note: taken as written
ST is the abbreviation for stone, the British unit of weight
taken as written

explanation.surface: A dog slips its leash and sprawls on a flagstone floor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lead' looks like a dog's leash but means the first letter; 'floor' is a verb, as in 'the news floored me'.
explanation.definitionFit: To floor someone is to stun or bewilder them completely, which is to astonish or amaze.

clue.text: Periodically forgetting strange name

indicators.note: forgetting something at regular intervals leaves every other letter out

parts.note: second, fourth and sixth letters

explanation.surface: Someone keeps forgetting an unusual name.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Strange' looks like an adjective describing the name, but it supplies the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A tag is a label or identifying nickname, so as a noun it can stand for a name.

clue.text: Some good news about goal

indicators.note: turning about means facing the other way, so the letters run backwards
some means a portion of the whole, so the letters sit inside the phrase

parts.note: across the join of the two words

explanation.surface: A sports report with good news about a goal being scored.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Goal' suggests football, but it means an aim or objective.
explanation.definitionFit: An end is the aim or purpose you are working towards, as in 'the end justifies the means'.

clue.text: Fancy any old guy or girl

indicators.note: fancy means elaborate or fanciful, so the letters are worked into a new pattern

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Asking whether you'd be attracted to just any bloke or a woman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fancy' reads as the British verb meaning to be attracted to, but it signals the rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: A young lady is a polite phrase for a girl or young woman, so the two are near-synonyms.
